title: In a line of four, who holds the power?
hook: The centre of three takes nearly all. In a line of four, how much do the inner two get?

knows: the centre of a 3-path takes all
Nash bargaining: each side gets its fallback plus half of what is left
doesNotKnow: that in a 4-path the inner people get 2/3, not all and not half

misconception: In a line of four, the two inner people have the same power as the centre of three, so take everything.
objective: The learner can explain why, in a line of four, each inner person's outside option depends on the other inner person's deal, so the balanced split settles at 2/3 for B and C and 1/3 for A and D.

claims.text: In the line A–B–C–D with deals A–B and C–D worth $1 each, the balanced outcome gives B and C $0.667 (two thirds) each and A and D $0.333.
claims.source: Balance: v_B = o_B + (1 − o_B)/2 with o_B = 1 − v_C (A's fallback is 0); by symmetry v = 1 − v/2, so v = 2/3. Fixed-point iteration in Demo.tsx shares() from 0.5: 0.75, 0.625, 0.6875, 0.6563 … within $0.0005 of 2/3 at round 9 (0.66699; round 8 is 0.66602, within $0.001 but shown as $0.666), so with TOL = 0.0005 SETTLED_AT = 9. Re-run in node by the builder (ncm-e02; re-run demo-builder 2026-10-14). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own node iteration v <- 1 - v/2 from 0.5: 0.75 0.625 0.6875 0.6563 0.6719 0.6641 0.6680 0.6660 0.6670 ... -> 2/3; A = 1/3. Correction to this source: within $0.001 of 2/3 at round 8 (|e8| = 1/1536), not 9, so SETTLED_AT = 8 (Demo comment '// 9' is stale; see c6). | Builder fix (demo-builder, 2026-10-14): W-214: TOL tightened to 0.0005, so 'settled' is round 9 and the source's round number is now right; Demo comment updated. Claim text unchanged. | FC pass 23 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node copy of shares() with TOL = 0.0005: 0.75, 0.625, 0.6875, 0.65625, ..., round 8 0.66602 (outside TOL), round 9 0.66699 (inside), rounds 10-14 stay inside. SETTLED_AT = 9, which matches the source and the Demo comment at line 34. Fixed point v = 1 - v/2 gives 2/3, and A = 1/3. Readouts at round 9 and later: B $0.667, A $0.333.

claims.text: Each round, every pair covers both people's fallbacks and halves the rest; B's fallback is what C would leave B in a B–C deal, $1 minus C's share.
claims.source: Definition of a balanced outcome (each matched pair splits its surplus over the two outside options equally): Easley and Kleinberg (2010) ch. 12; Cook and Yamagishi (1992). Round-by-round updating is the lesson's way of showing the fixed point, a simplification; stage chip 'Model: each pair covers both fallbacks, then halves the rest'. Fact-checker confirms the definition and attribution. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Definition matches the balanced outcome (Nash bargaining split with network outside options) in Easley & Kleinberg ch. 12 'Bargaining and Power in Networks' (chapter title confirmed by search snippet of the ToC; book host blocked; section placement from my own knowledge, confident) which credits Cook & Yamagishi (1992) for the concept (from memory, not opened). Round-by-round update is disclosed on the stage chip as the lesson's model. | Builder (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, wave H, v5): stage chip changed: after the commit it now reads 'Round 0: no fallbacks yet, each pair halves $1' at round 0 and 'Round N: B's fallback = $1 − C's last share x = y' after; the locked chip is unchanged. Reopened: unverified. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Learner text describes the lesson's own rule, checked against Demo.tsx v5 shares(): oB = 1 - vC (C's last share), vB = oB + (1 - oB)/2 (A's fallback 0, so cover both, halve the rest). Chip: locked 'Each pair covers both fallbacks, then halves the rest'; round 0 'no fallbacks yet, each pair halves $1'; round N 'B's fallback = $1 − C's last share x = y'. All match. The Easley and Kleinberg / Cook and Yamagishi attribution in the source field was NOT opened (hosts unreachable) and is not in learner text; it is not the basis of this verdict.

claims.text: In a line of three, the centre's two partners have no other deal, so the centre can take nearly all.
claims.source: 3-path network exchange: the end nodes' only option is the centre, so stable outcomes give the centre the whole $1 (Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 12; lesson middle-of-three-takes-all). claims.text: B's fallback is $1 minus C's last share, and C's mirrors B's: C got $0.750 in round 1, so B's fallback was $0.250 in round 2.
claims.source: Demo.tsx shares(): oB = 1 - vC (previous round); the line is symmetric (A-B and C-D both worth $1, A and D have no fallback), so vB = vC every round. Round 1 vC = 0.75, round 2 oB = 0.25. The stage chip prints 'B's fallback = $1 − C's last share ...' each round and the trace row 'B's fallback: .000 .500 .250 ...'. Builder's Node run, 2026-10-14. Model rule, not a forecast (c5). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 24): VERIFIED. Own run: round 1 share 0.75 (C = B by symmetry), round 2 fallback 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 -> '$0.250'. Chip 'B's fallback = $1 − C's last share' matches. | Builder (demo-builder, 2026-10-14, wave H, v5): reveal sentence shortened; the stage chip now reads 'Round N: B's fallback = $1 − C's last share ...' and the readouts row is gone (trace rows unchanged). Reopened: unverified. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own run tracking vB and vC separately: equal every round (symmetry). Round 1 C = 0.75 -> '$0.750'; round 2 fallback 1 - 0.75 = 0.25 -> '$0.250' (reveal uses ROUNDS[1].inner and ROUNDS[2].fallback). Trace row 'B's fallback: .000 .500 .250 ...'.

claims.text: Hook: 'The centre of three takes nearly all.'
claims.source: 3-path network exchange: the end nodes' only option is the centre, so stable outcomes give the centre the whole $1 (Easley and Kleinberg 2010 ch. 12; lesson middle-of-three-takes-all); carried from withdrawn c4, which the fact-checker confirmed in pass 22. Added by demo-builder 2026-10-14 (wave H, v5): the hook sentence had no claim of its own. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Verified as a derivation under the lesson's own rule, not on the cited source (not opened). 3-path A-B-C with A-B matched: C has no deal (share 0), so B's fallback is 1 - 0 = 1 and B gets 1 + 0/2 = $1 (own node). 'Nearly all' is weaker than 'all', so it holds; c5 frames it as a model.

claims.text: Each inner person's option feeds the other's, so neither takes all: power depends on the network.
claims.source: Demo.tsx shares(): oB = 1 − vC and oC = 1 − vB, so each inner person's fallback is set by the other's share; the fixed point is 2/3 each, not 1 (c1). 'Power depends on the network' contrasts with the 3-path (c8), where the centre gets nearly all with the same count of two partners. Reveal paragraph 3, v5 (demo-builder, 2026-10-14). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation: oB = 1 - vC and oC = 1 - vB in shares(), so each inner fallback is set by the other's share; fixed point v = 1 - v/2 = 2/3 < 1 (own run converges to 0.66666). Contrast with the 3-path (c8) where the centre gets 1. 'Power depends on the network' is the lesson's interpretive conclusion from that contrast, consistent with the model.

recall.question: In a line A–B–C–D, A–B and C–D each split $1, and each pair covers both fallbacks then halves the rest. Why doesn't B take nearly all, as the centre of a line of three would?
options: B's fallback is a deal with C, and C has a good fallback too, so B can't squeeze C
recall.why: B's outside option is whatever C would leave B, and C's is whatever B would leave C. Neither is desperate, so the split settles at 2/3 to 1/3.
